stages.name: Fiscal deficits over the cycle
stages.title: Fiscal deficits over the cycle
stages.sub: Why deficits grow and shrink with the economy, and what else drives their size.

steps.q: A recession hits. More people lose their jobs and claim benefits, while fewer people earn enough to pay tax. What happens to government spending and tax revenue, without any new policy being announced?
steps.right: Spending rises and revenue falls automatically
steps.wrong: Spending and revenue both stay fixed until a new budget
steps.hint: Benefits and tax revenue respond to how many people are working, not to a new announcement.
steps.pre: Government spending and tax revenue that move with the cycle on their own are called

steps.q: During that recession, benefit spending rises and tax revenue falls, both because output has fallen below its normal level. What happens to the budget deficit purely because of this downturn?
steps.right: It widens because of the downturn itself
steps.wrong: It stays the same because policy hasn't changed
steps.hint: Higher spending plus lower revenue, with nothing else changing, means what for the gap between them?

steps.q: Now imagine the economy recovers fully and is producing at its normal, full-capacity level, yet the government is still spending more than it raises in tax every year. Is this gap explained by the state of the cycle?
steps.right: No, it remains even at full capacity
steps.wrong: Yes, it will close once the recovery is complete
steps.hint: The economy has already returned to normal in this scenario, so what's causing the leftover gap?

steps.q: Two countries are both in recession, but one has an ageing population needing far more pensions and healthcare regardless of the cycle, and one government also decides to cut tax rates. Would the size of their deficits be explained by the downturn alone?
steps.right: No, ageing costs and tax decisions matter too
steps.wrong: Yes, the downturn alone explains the whole deficit
steps.hint: Think about what else, besides the cyclical and structural split, could push a deficit up or down: policy choices, demographics, interest payments.
